# Vignette: Fatima, Age 71

Fatima has lived in this country for nearly thirty years, long enough to have raised other people's children as tenderly as she once raised her own. She is a nanny — has been for most of her adult life here — and there is something in the work that has always steadied her. Small hands reaching for hers. The reliable rhythm of school pickups, afternoon snacks, bedtime stories. She knows how to be calm for children. She has had to be.

Two years ago, Fatima was walking home from the bus stop on a Tuesday afternoon in early November when she witnessed a car strike a young woman crossing the street directly in front of her. The woman — perhaps twenty-five, carrying grocery bags — was thrown several feet and lay motionless on the pavement. Fatima ran to her. She knelt beside the woman and held her hand, speaking softly in Arabic, then in English, pressing her scarf against a wound on the woman's head. She stayed like that until the ambulance came. She does not know whether the woman survived. She has never been able to find out, and this uncertainty has become its own particular torment.

In the days that followed, Fatima told herself she was fine. She went to work. She packed lunches and read picture books and walked the children to the park. But she began crossing streets differently — pausing far longer than necessary at curbs, gripping the hands of the children so tightly that the older one once looked up at her and asked if something was wrong. She told him no. She has become skilled at saying no.

At night, the skill fails her. She wakes between two and four in the morning with a physical certainty that something terrible is happening — her heart hammering, her nightgown damp, the images returning with a vividness that makes them feel like the present rather than the past. She sees the woman's grocery bags split open on the pavement, oranges rolling into the gutter. She sees the blood on her own scarf, which she threw away but cannot stop seeing. Her husband, Karim, wakes with her and brings water and sits beside her, and she is grateful for this, though she cannot fully explain to him what she is experiencing. He was not there. She is not sure language can carry what she saw.

During the day, Fatima moves through a version of her life that feels slightly removed from her, as though she is watching herself from a short distance. She finds it difficult to feel pleasure in things that once brought her joy — cooking on weekends, video calls with her grandchildren in Amman, the small ceremonies of her faith. She prays, but the peace that prayer used to bring her does not come the way it once did. She sits on her prayer rug and the images arrive anyway.

She has begun avoiding the block where the accident happened, which means a longer walk to the bus stop, which means leaving the house earlier, which means less sleep. She is aware of the logic of this arrangement and does not like it, but she cannot make herself walk past that intersection. She tried once, in the spring, and stood frozen at the corner for several minutes before turning back.

What troubles Fatima most — more than the nightmares, more than the detours — is what the experience has done to her sense of herself as a person who can help. She held that young woman's hand. She stayed. And still she does not know if it was enough. She carries the children in her care with the same devotion she always has, perhaps even more fiercely now, but underneath the steadiness she has always offered them, something has shifted. She knows, in a way she did not know before, how quickly a person can be there and then not there. She knows it in her body, in the place where sleep used to live.
